<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm: homotopy fixed points}
Let $G$ be a discrete group. We have the following relationships:
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{{\mathsf{dTC}}}_r(G)&\geq \operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{{\mathcal P}_r}(G^r)\\
\operatorname{{\mathsf{dcat}}}(G)&\geq \operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{\mathcal{FIN}}(G)\\
\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_r(G)&=\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{\mathcal{D}_r}(G^r)\\
\operatorname{{\mathsf{cat}}}(G)&=\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{\{1\}}(G).
\end{align*}
Here, the families $\mathcal{D}_r$ and ${\mathcal P}_r$ are the diagonal and permutational families of Definitions~\ref{def: diagonal family} and~\ref{def: permutational family}, respectively, and $\mathcal{FIN}$ is the family of all finite subgroups.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor: equality impermutable}
For every $r>1$, we have $\operatorname{{\mathsf{dTC}}}_r(G)=\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_r(G)$ for $G$ torsion-free nilpotent, torsion-free hyperbolic, uniquely divisible, bi-orderable, or residually any of these.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm: subgroup lower bound}
Fix a natural number $r>1$ and a torsion-free subgroup $K\leq G^r$. If the intersection of $K$ with every conjugate of the diagonal subgroup is trivial, then 
\[\operatorname{{\mathsf{dTC}}}_r(G)\geq \operatorname{{\mathsf{cd}}}(K).\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
We have $\operatorname{{\mathsf{dTC}}}_r(G)=\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{{\mathcal P}_r}(G^r)$ for every torsion-free group $G$ and $r>1$.
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
Is there a torsion-free group $G$ and $r>1$ such that one of the inequalities  $\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{{\mathcal P}_r}(G^r)\leq \operatorname{{\mathsf{dTC}}}_r(G)\leq \operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_r(G)=\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{\mathcal{D}_r}(G^r)$ is strict?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def: model}
A set $\mathcal{F}$ of subgroups of $G$ is called a \emph{family} if it is closed under the formation of conjugates and finite intersections.\footnote{Some references require a family to be closed under the formation of subgroups. Following~\cite{Lu,FGLO}, we do not impose this requirement.} We say that a $G$-complex $X$ has \emph{isotropy in} $\mathcal{F}$ if the stabilizer $G_x$ lies in $\mathcal{F}$ for every $x\in X$. We say that $X$ is a \emph{model for (the classifying space of}) $\mathcal{F}$ if
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $X$ has isotropy in $\mathcal{F}$, and
    \item any $G$-complex $Y$ with isotropy in $\mathcal{F}$ admits an equivariant map to $X$, unique up to equivariant homotopy.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm: luck}
    Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of subgroups. A $G$-complex $X$ is a model for $\mathcal{F}$ if and only if
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $X$ has isotropy in $\mathcal{F}$, and
        \item the fixed point set $X^H$ of $X$ is weakly contractible for each $H\in\mathcal{F}$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem: skeleta of models}
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of subgroups of $G$ and $X$ and $Y$ be two models for $\mathcal{F}$. For any $n\geq0$, there are equivariant cellular maps $X_n\to Y_n\to X_n$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
By our assumption on $X$ and $Y$, there are essentially unique equivariant cellular maps $X\to Y\to X$, and restricting to $n$-skeleta yields the result.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop: restriction family}
The set $\varphi^*\mathcal{F}$ is a family and $\varphi^*E_\mathcal{F}(G)$ is a model for $\varphi^*\mathcal{F}$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Closure under intersection is immediate from the fact that the preimages and intersections commute. 
For closure under conjugation, given $H\in \mathcal{F}$ and $k\in K$, the inclusion $\varphi^{-1}(H)^k\subseteq \varphi^{-1}(H^{\varphi(k)})$ is immediate. Since the latter subgroup lies in $\varphi^*\mathcal{F}$, it suffices to demonstrate the reverse inclusion. Given $a\in K$ and $h\in H$ with $\varphi(a)=h^{\varphi(k)}$, rearranging grants that $a^{k^{-1}}\in \varphi^{-1}(H)$, so $a\in \varphi^{-1}(H)^k$, as desired.

For the second claim, since we are dealing with discrete groups, the restriction $\varphi^*E_\mathcal{F}(G)$ is a $K$-CW complex, and we have $K_x=\varphi^{-1}(G_x)$ and $\varphi^*E_\mathcal{F}(G)^{\varphi^{-1}(H)}=E_\mathcal{F}(G)^H$, so the validity of the criteria of Theorem~\ref{thm: luck} for the restriction follows from that of the corresponding criteria for $E_\mathcal{F}(G)$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- ex-1: body_md -->
\label{ex: singleton}
    The family of all subgroups of $G$ is modeled by a singleton.
<!-- end ex-1 -->
<!-- ex-2: body_md -->
\label{ex: trivial}
The family $\{1\}$ comprising only the trivial subgroup is modeled by the universal cover $EG$ of $BG$.
<!-- end ex-2 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def: diagonal family}
The $r$th \emph{diagonal family} is the family $\mathcal{D}_r=\mathcal{D}_r(G)$ of subgroups of $G^r$ generated by the trivial subgroup and the image of the diagonal homomorphism $G\to G^r$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm: fglo}
The infinite join $(G^{r-1})^{\star \infty}$ is a model for $\mathcal{D}_r$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop: simplex over G}
The barycentric subdivision of the simplex $\Delta^{G}$ is a model for $\mathcal{FIN}$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem: barycentric}
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of subgroups of $G$ and $X$ a simplicial complex with a simplicial $G$-action. If $X$ satisfies the two conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm: luck}, then the barycentric subdivision of $X$ is a model for $\mathcal{F}$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem: convex}
Let $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex subspace with an affine linear $G$-action. For any subgroup $H\leq G$, the fixed set $X^H$ is convex.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem: barycentric}, it suffices to verify the criteria of Theorem~\ref{thm: luck} for $\Delta^G$. For the first criterion, supposing that $g$ fixes $\sum_{i=1}^n t_i g_i$ with the $g_i$ distinct, it follows that $\{g_i\}_{i=1}^n=\{gg_i\}_{i=1}^n$ so $g\in\{g_1g_i^{-1}\}_{i=1}^n$, a finite set. For the second criterion, since every fixed set is convex by Lemma~\ref{lem: convex}, it suffices to note that the fixed set of $H$ is non-empty for finite $H$, since $H$ fixes the barycenter of the face spanned by $H$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop: G-CW criterion}
A CW complex $X$ with a cellular $G$-action is a $G$-complex if and only if, for every $g\in G$, any open cell $e$ fixed setwise by $g$ is fixed pointwise by $g$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor: barycentric}
Let $X$ be a simplicial complex with a simplicial $G$-action. The barycentric subdivision of $X$ with its canonical $G$-action is a $G$-complex.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
An open $n$-simplex $\sigma$ of the barycentric subdivision is indexed by a chain $\sigma_0\subsetneq \cdots\subsetneq \sigma_n$ of simplices of $X$, and $g\sigma$ is the simplex indexed by $g\sigma_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq g\sigma_n$. Assuming that $g\sigma=\sigma$, it follows that $g\sigma_i=\sigma_i$ for each $0\leq i\leq n$, so $g$ fixes the vertices of $\sigma$. Since the action is simplicial, it follows that $g$ fixes $\sigma$ pointwise, and Proposition~\ref{prop: G-CW criterion} applies.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def: main definition}
Let $G$ be a group and $\mathcal{F}$ a family of subgroups of $G$. The \emph{$\mathcal{F}$-topological complexity of $G$} is the quantity
\[\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)=\min\left\{n\ge 0\ \middle| \ E_{\mathcal{F}}(G)_{n}^{hG} \ne \varnothing \right\}.\]
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop: atc char-2}
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of subgroups containing the trivial subgroup. The quantity $\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)$ is the least extended natural number $n$ for which the canonical map $EG=E_{\{1\}}(G)\to E_\mathcal{F}(G)$ factors through $E_\mathcal{F}(G)_n$ up to equivariant homotopy.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By definition, $\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)\leq n$ if and only if there is an equivariant map $EG\to E_\mathcal{F}(G)_n$. The result of composing this map with the inclusion into $E_\mathcal{F}(G)$ is homotopic to the canonical map by Definition~\ref{def: model}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- ex-3: body_md -->
When $\mathcal{F}$ is the family of all subgroups, we have $\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)=0$ by Example~\ref{ex: singleton}.
<!-- end ex-3 -->
<!-- ex-4: body_md -->
\label{example: trivial family cd}
In view of Example~\ref{ex: trivial}, we have $\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{\{1\}}(G)=\operatorname{{\mathsf{cd}}}(G)$, the cohomological dimension of $G$. Indeed, by Example~\ref{ex: trivial} and Proposition~\ref{prop: atc char-2}, the left-hand quantity is the least $n$ for which the $n$-skeleton of $EG$ is a homotopy retract. That this latter number is the cohomological dimension is a well-known fact, which may be proven by the same argument as~\cite[Thm. 7.4]{KW1}, for example.
<!-- end ex-4 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop: functorial bounds}
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of subgroups of $G$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For any subfamily $\mathcal{F}'\subseteq \mathcal{F}$, we have $\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)\leq \operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{\mathcal{F}'}(G)$.
\item For any homomorphism $\varphi: K\to G$, we have $\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{\varphi^*\mathcal{F}}(K)\leq \operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For the first claim, setting $n=\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{\mathcal{F}'}(G)$, the definition grants the existence of an equivariant map $EG\to E_{\mathcal{F}'}(G)_n$. Composing this map with the restriction to $n$-skeleta of the essentially unique map $E_{\mathcal{F}'}(G)\to E_{\mathcal{F}}(G)$, we conclude that $\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)\leq n$, as desired. For the second claim, setting $n=\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)$, the definition grants the existence of a $G$-equivariant map $EG\to E_\mathcal{F}(G)_n$. Composing with the natural map from $EK$,
we obtain the $K$-equivariant map
$EK\to \varphi^*EG\to \varphi^*E_\mathcal{F}(G)_n,$ so $\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{\varphi^*\mathcal{F}}(K)\leq n$ by Proposition~\ref{prop: restriction family}, as desired.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor: general subgroup lower bound}
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of subgroups of $G$ and $K\leq G$ a subgroup. If $K\cap H=\{1\}$ for every $H\in \mathcal{F}$, then
\[\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)\geq \operatorname{{\mathsf{cd}}}(K).\]
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Writing $i:K\to G$ for the inclusion, the assumption grants that $i^*\mathcal{F}=\{1\}$, so the conclusion follows from Example~\ref{example: trivial family cd} and Proposition~\ref{prop: functorial bounds}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of subgroups of $G$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The \emph{geometric dimension} of $G$ with respect to $\mathcal{F}$ is the least extended natural number $\mathsf{gd}_\mathcal{F}(G)$ such that $\mathcal{F}$ admits a model of dimension $\mathsf{gd}_\mathcal{F}(G)$.
\item The \emph{cohomological dimension} of $G$ with respect to $\mathcal{F}$ is the least extended natural number $\operatorname{{\mathsf{cd}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)$ such that $H^n_\mathcal{F}(G;M)=0$ for every coefficient system $M$ and $n>\operatorname{{\mathsf{cd}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)$.
\item The \emph{principal component dimension} of $G$ with respect to $\mathcal{F}$ is the least extended natural number $\mathsf{pcd}_\mathcal{F}(G)$ such that the restriction homomorphism $H^n_\mathcal{F}(EG;M)\to H^n(G;M(G))$ induced by the inclusion of the trivial family vanishes for every coefficient system $M$ and $n>\mathsf{pcd}_\mathcal{F}(M)$. If $1\notin\mathcal{F}$, then $\mathsf{pcd}_\mathcal{F}(G)$ is undefined.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop: cohomological bounds}
For any group $G$ and family of subgroups $\mathcal{F}$ containing the trivial subgroup, we have the inequalities
\[\mathsf{pcd}_\mathcal{F}(G)\leq  \operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)\leq \mathsf{gd}_\mathcal{F}(G)\leq \max \{3, \operatorname{{\mathsf{cd}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)\}.\]
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The rightmost inequality is~\cite[Theorem~5.2]{Lu}. For the middle inequality, choosing a model for $\mathcal{F}$ of dimension $n=\mathsf{gd}_\mathcal{F}(G)$, the assumption that $1\in\mathcal{F}$ grants the existence of an essentially unique equivariant cellular map $EG=E_{\{1\}}(G)\to E_\mathcal{F}(G)=E_\mathcal{F}(G)_n$, as desired. For the leftmost inequality, set $n=\mathsf{pcd}_\mathcal{F}(G)$, and suppose that $\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_\mathcal{F}(G)<n$. From the definitions and Proposition~\ref{prop: atc char-2}, there is a coefficient system $M$ for which the restriction homomorphism $H^n_\mathcal{F}(G;M)\to H^n_\mathcal{F}(EG;M)$ is nontrivial and a commutative diagram of the form
\[
\xymatrix{
H^n_\mathcal{F}(EG;M)   & & 
H^n_{\mathcal{F}}(E_{\mathcal{F}}(G); M) \ar[ll] \ar[dl]
\\
& H^n_{\mathcal{F}}(E_{\mathcal{F}}(G)_{n-1}; M).\ar[ul] 
}
\]
Since $E_{\mathcal{F}}(G)_{n-1}$ is $(n-1)$-dimensional, the group at the bottom of this diagram vanishes, so the top homomorphism is trivial by commutativity, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem: cosets}
There is a canonical isomorphism of $G^r$-sets of the form
\[G^r/G\cong G^{r-1}.\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
By orbit-stabilizer, it suffices to show that the action of $G^r$ on $G^{r-1}$ is transitive, and that the stabilizer of $\widehat 1\in G^{r-1}$ is the diagonal subgroup. For transitivity, we have $(1, g_1^{-1},\ldots, g_{r-1}^{-1})\widehat 1=(g_1,\ldots, g_{r-1}),$ while requiring that $(g, h_1,\ldots, h_{r-1})$ stabilize $\widehat 1$ is equivalent to requiring that $gh_i^{-1}=1$ for each $i$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def: type sigma}
    Fix subset $T\subseteq G^{r-1}$ and a permutation $\sigma\in \Sigma_{T}$. We say that an element $g\in G$ is of \emph{type $\sigma$} if
    \[
    \sigma(x)\sigma(y)^{-1}\widehat g=\widehat gxy^{-1}
    \]
    for all $x,y\in T$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop: subgroup}
    For any subset $T\subseteq G^{r-1}$ and subgroup $H\leq \Sigma_{T}$, the subset $\Delta({ T},{ H})\subseteq G^{r}$ is a subgroup.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Given  $ g$ of type $\sigma$ and  $h$ of type $\tau$, a straightforward verification shows that $gh$ is of type $\sigma\tau$ and that $g_\sigma h_\tau=(gh)_{\sigma\tau}$. It is likewise straightforward to verify that $g^{-1}$ is of type $\sigma^{-1}$ and that $(g_\sigma)^{-1}=(g^{-1})_{\sigma^{-1}}$. The claim now follows upon observing that the set in question is nonempty, since $1$ is of type $\textup{id}$ and $1_\mathrm{id}=1$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def: permutational family}
The $r$th \emph{permutational family} ${\mathcal P}_r={\mathcal P}_r(G)$ is the set comprising the trivial subgroup and all subgroups of $G^{r}$ of the form $\Delta({ T},{{\Sigma}}_{{{\alpha}}})$, where $T$ ranges over finite subsets of $G^{r-1}$ and $\alpha$ over partitions of $T$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop: family}
For any $r>1$, the set ${\mathcal P}_r$ is a family of subgroups.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem: intersection}
Given subsets $S,T\subseteq G^{r-1}$ and permutations $\sigma\in \Sigma_{S}$ and $\tau\in\Sigma_{T}$, we have
\[
\Delta(S,{{\sigma}})\cap\Delta(T,{{\tau}})=
     \begin{cases}
\Delta(S\cup T,{{\sigma}}\cup{{\tau}}) & \text{ if }\sigma|_{S\cap T}=\tau|_{S\cap T}
        \\
        \varnothing & \text{ otherwise},
    \end{cases}   
\]
where $\sigma\cup\tau\in\Sigma_{S\cup T}$ is the unique permutation on $S\cup T$ restricting to $\sigma$ on $S$ and to $\tau$ on $T$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Given $x\in S\cap T$, any element of the intersection in question has the form 
\[(g, \sigma(x)^{-1}\widehat gx)=(g,\tau(x)^{-1}\widehat g x),\] and rearranging yields the equation $\sigma(x)=\tau(x)$. Thus, we may assume that $\sigma|_{S\cap T}=\tau|_{S\cap T}$, writing  $\rho=\sigma\cup\tau$ for brevity. In this case, an element $g$ is of type $\rho$ if and only if $g$ is both of type $\sigma$ and of type $\tau$, and $(g,g_\sigma)=(g,g_\rho)=(g,g_\tau)$ for such $g$, implying the claim.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem: meet inclusion}
Fix a set $X$, finite subsets $S,T\subseteq X$ with respective partitions $\alpha$ and $\beta$, and permutations $\sigma\in \Sigma_S$ and $\tau\in \Sigma_T$. If $\sigma|_{S\cap T}=\tau|_{S\cap T}$, then $\sigma\cup\tau\in \Sigma_{\alpha\wedge\beta}$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The claim is that $\sigma\cup \tau$ preserves the blocks of $\alpha\wedge\beta$. Now, these blocks are of three types: first, blocks of $\alpha$ lying in $S\setminus T$; second, blocks of $\beta$ lying in $T\setminus S$; and, third, intersections of blocks of $\alpha$ and blocks of $\beta$ lying in $S\cap T$. In the first case, $\sigma\cup\tau$ acts as $\sigma$, which preserves the blocks of $\alpha$ and preserves $S\setminus T$ by assumption. The second case is similar. In the third case, $\sigma\cup \tau$ acts equally as $\sigma$ and as $\tau$, hence preserves the blocks of $\alpha$ and of $\beta$, and preserves $S\cap T$ by assumption.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor: intersection meet}
Given finite subsets $S,T\subseteq G^r$ with respective partitions $\alpha$ and $\beta$, we have $\Delta(S,\Sigma_\alpha)\cap \Delta(T,\Sigma_\beta)=\Delta(S\cup T, \Sigma_{\alpha\wedge \beta})$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The rightward inclusion follows from Lemmas~\ref{lem: intersection} and~\ref{lem: meet inclusion}, in view of the equality
\[
\Delta(S,{{\Sigma}}_{{{\alpha}}})\cap \Delta(T,{{\Sigma}}_{{{\beta}}})=\bigcup_{\substack{{{\sigma}}\in{{\Sigma}}_{{{\alpha}}}\\ {{\tau}}\in{{\Sigma}}_{{{\beta}}}}} \Delta(S,{{\sigma}})\cap \Delta(T,{{\tau}}).
\] On the other hand, writing $\overline \alpha=\alpha\cup\{T\setminus S\}$, we have $\Sigma_{\alpha\wedge\beta}\leq \Sigma_{\overline\alpha}$ and $\Delta(S\cup T,\Sigma_{\overline\alpha})\subseteq\Delta(S, \Sigma_\alpha)$, implying the reverse inclusion.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Closure under intersection is immediate from Corollary~\ref{cor: intersection meet}. As for conjugation, fix a finite subset $T\subseteq G^{r-1}$, a permutation $\sigma\in \Sigma_T$, and an arbitrary element $(h,k)\in G\times G^{r-1}$. Defining $\widetilde T=\widehat hTk^{-1}$, we obtain a permutation $\widetilde\sigma\in \Sigma_{\widetilde T}$ by the formula $\widetilde \sigma(\widehat hxk^{-1})=\widehat h\sigma(x)k^{-1}$. With these definitions, a direct verification shows that $g$ is of type $\sigma$ if and only if $g^h$ is of type $\widetilde \sigma$, and that $(g,g_\sigma)^{(h,k)}=(g^h, (g^h)_{\widetilde \sigma})$, whence $\Delta(T,\sigma)^{(h,k)}=\Delta(\widetilde T,\widetilde \sigma)$. In the same way, a partition $\alpha$ of $T$ determines a partition $\widetilde \alpha$ of $\widetilde T$, and it follows that $\Delta(T,\Sigma_{\alpha})^{(h,k)}=\Delta(\widetilde T,\Sigma_{\widetilde \alpha})\in {\mathcal P}_r$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop: diagonal equivalence}
A subgroup of $G^r$ lies in $\mathcal{D}_r$ if and only if it is of the form $\Delta(T,\textup{id})$ for some finite subset $T\subseteq G^{r-1}$. In particular, the family $\mathcal{D}_r$ is a subfamily of ${\mathcal P}_r$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
It is shown in~\cite{FGLO} for $r=2$ and~\cite{FO} in general that a non-trivial subgroup of $G^{r}$ lies in $\mathcal{D}_r$ if and only if it is of the form \[
H_{x,S}:=\left\{\left(g,x\widehat gx^{-1}\right)\ \middle| \ \widehat g\in Z(S) \right\} \leq G^{r}.
\] for some $x\in G^{r-1}$ and finite $S\subseteq G^{r-1}$. For the ``if direction'', choose a finite set $T\subseteq G^{r-1}$, and set $S=\{xy^{-1}\mid x,y\in T\}$. Then we have $Z(T,\textup{id})=\{g\in G\mid \widehat g\in Z(S)\}$ and $\Delta(T,\textup{id})=H_{x,S}$ by inspection. For the ``only if'' direction, it follows from Lemma~\ref{lem: intersection} and the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop: family} concerning conjugates that the set of subgroups of the form $\Delta(T,\textup{id})$ is a family of subgroups. Thus, to establish that every member of $\mathcal{D}_r$ lies in this family, it suffices to show that the diagonal subgroup does so, but the diagonal subgroup is $\Delta(\{\,\widehat 1\,\}, \textup{id})$ by inspection.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm: classifying model}
The barycentric subdivision of the simplex $\Delta^{G^{r-1}}$ is a model for ${\mathcal P}_r$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem: measure stabilizer}
For $\mu\in \Delta^{G^{r-1}}$ with support $T$ and associated partition $\alpha$, the stabilizer subgroup of $\mu$ under the action of $G^{r}$ is $\Delta({ T},{{\Sigma}}_{{{\alpha}}})$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
We begin by writing $\mu=\sum_{x\in T}t_xx$. Given $\sigma\in \Sigma_\alpha$ and $g$ of type $\sigma$, we recall that $g_\sigma=\sigma(x)^{-1}\widehat gx$ for any $x\in T$, so 
\begin{align*}
(g,g_\sigma)\cdot \mu &= \sum_{x\in T}t_x \bigl(\widehat gx\bigl(\sigma(x)^{-1}\widehat gx\bigr)^{-1}\bigr)
=\sum_{x\in T}t_x \sigma(x)=\mu,
\end{align*}
where the last equality follows from our assumption on $\sigma$. It follows that $\Delta({ T},{{\Sigma}}_{{{\alpha}}})$ stabilizes $\mu$. Conversely, supposing that $(g,h)\in G\times G^{r-1}$ stabilizes $\mu$, it follows that, for each $x\in T$, we have $\widehat gxh^{-1}=z$ for some $z\in T$ with $t_x=t_z$. Thus, the formula $\sigma(x)=\widehat gx h^{-1}$ defines a permutation $\sigma\in \Sigma_\alpha$. Moreover, we have
\[
\sigma(x)\sigma(y)^{-1}\widehat g=\bigl(\widehat gxh^{-1}\bigr)\bigl(hy^{-1}\widehat g^{-1}\bigr)\widehat g=\widehat gxy^{-1},
    \] for $x,y\in T$, so $g$ has type $\sigma$, and rearranging the definition shows that $h=g_\sigma$, so $(g,h)\in \Delta(T,\Sigma_\alpha)$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem: designer measure}
For any finite subset $T\subseteq G^{r-1}$ and partition $\alpha$, there is a point $\mu\in\Delta^{G^{r-1}}$ with support $T$ and associated partition $\alpha$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Write $\alpha=\{A_i\}_{i=1}^\ell$ with $|A_i|$ non-increasing. Since $\sum_{i=1}^\ell i=\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{2}$, the expression 
$\mu=\sum_{i=1}^\ell \sum_{x\in A_i} \frac{2i}{\ell(\ell+1)|A_i|} x$ defines an element of $\Delta^{G^r}$ with support $T$. To see that $\alpha$ is the partition associated to $\mu$, note that, for $i<j$, we have 
\[\frac{2i}{\ell(\ell+1)|A_i|}<\frac{2j}{\ell(\ell+1)|A_i|}\leq \frac{2j}{\ell(\ell+1)|A_j|},\] since $|A_i|$ is non-increasing. In particular, elements of $T$ have common coefficient in $\mu$ if and only if they lie in the same block of $\alpha$, as claimed.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem: barycentric}, it suffices to verify the criteria of Theorem~\ref{thm: luck}. Lemma~\ref{lem: measure stabilizer} implies that $\Delta^{G^{r-1}}$ has isotropy in ${\mathcal P}_r$. Since the same result together with Lemma~\ref{lem: designer measure} implies that the fixed point set $(\Delta^{G^{r-1}})^H$ is non-empty for every $H\in{\mathcal P}_r$, the proof is complete upon noting that this set is also convex by Lemma~\ref{lem: convex}.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def: secat}
Let $f:X\to Y$ be a map of topological spaces. The \emph{sectional category} of $f$, denoted $\operatorname{{\mathsf{secat}}}(f)$, is the least $n$ for which there is an open cover $\{U_i\}_{i=0}^n$ of $Y$ such that $f$ admits a local section over each $U_i$.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem: join secat}
Let $p:E\to B$ be a Serre fibration. If $B$ is paracompact, then $\operatorname{{\mathsf{secat}}}(p)\leq n$ if and only if the induced map $E^{\star(n+1)}_B \to B$ admits a section.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- ex-5: body_md -->
\label{ex: simplex}
If $X$ is discrete, then $\mathcal{B}_m(X)\cong\Delta^X_{m-1}$, the $(m-1)$-skeleton of the simplex spanned by $X$.
<!-- end ex-5 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
Let $f:X\to Y$ be a map. The \emph{distributional sectional category} of $f$, denoted $\operatorname{{\mathsf{dsecat}}}(f)$, is the least $n$ for which the induced map $\mathcal{B}_{n+1}(f)\to Y$ admits a section.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem: secat homotopy}
Consider the following commutative diagram of maps between topological spaces:
\[
\xymatrix{
E_1\ar[dr]_-{p_1}\ar[rr]&&E_2\ar[dl]^-{p_2}\\
&B.
}
\] If the diagonal maps are Hurewicz fibrations and the horizontal map a homotopy equivalence, then $\operatorname{{\mathsf{secat}}}(p_1)=\operatorname{{\mathsf{secat}}}(p_2)$ and $\operatorname{{\mathsf{dsecat}}}(p_2)=\operatorname{{\mathsf{dsecat}}}(p_2)$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The first claim follows from \cite[Prop.~2.1]{Rud}, and the second is a special case of~\cite[Prop. 5.2]{KW1}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a group. We write $\pi^1_G:BG^{[0,1]}\to BG$ for the map given by evaluation at $0$. For $r>1$, we write $\pi_G^r:BG^{[0,1]}\to BG^r$ for the map with $i$th coordinate given by evaluation at $\frac{i-1}{r-1}$. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item The \emph{category} of $G$ is $\operatorname{{\mathsf{cat}}}(G)=\operatorname{{\mathsf{secat}}}(\pi^1_G)$.
\item The \emph{distributional category} of $G$ is $\operatorname{{\mathsf{dcat}}}(G)=\operatorname{{\mathsf{dsecat}}}(\pi^1_G)$.
\item The $r$th \emph{sequential topological complexity} of $G$ is $\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_r(G)=\operatorname{{\mathsf{secat}}}(\pi_G^r)$.
\item The $r$th \emph{sequential distributional topological complexity} of $G$ is $\operatorname{{\mathsf{dTC}}}_r(G)=\operatorname{{\mathsf{dsecat}}}(\pi_G^r)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem: path space borel}
For any $r>1$, there is a commutative diagram of the following form, in which the horizontal arrow is a homotopy equivalence:
\[\xymatrix{
BG^{[0,1]}\ar[rr]\ar[dr]_-{\pi_G^r}&&EG^r/G\ar[dl]\\
&BG^r.
}\]
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Consider the following commutative solid diagram of maps between topological spaces:
\[\xymatrix{
EG\ar[d]\ar[r]&EG^r\ar[d]\\
BG\ar[d]_-i\ar[r]&EG^r/G\ar[d]\\
BG^{[0,1]}\ar@{-->}[ur]\ar[r]^-{\pi_G^r}&BG^r.
}\] Here, we have written $i$ for the inclusion of the constant paths, the top arrow is the diagonal map, which is $G$-equivariant, and the middle horizontal arrow is the map induced on $G$-orbits. Now, the lower right-hand vertical map is a fiber bundle, hence a Hurewicz fibration, and, since $BG$ is a CW complex, the map $i$ is a trivial Hurewicz cofibration; therefore, the indicated dashed filler exists. Since the top arrow is a weak equivalence with free action on source and target, the induced map $BG\to EG^r/G$ is also a weak equivalence, hence a homotopy equivalence by the Whitehead theorem. The claim now follows by two-out-of-three.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem: fiber bundles}
Let $p:E\to B$ be a fiber bundle with fiber $F$ and structure group $K$, and fix $n>0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The induced map $E_B^{\star n}\to B$ is a fiber bundle with fiber $F^{\star n}$ and structure group $K$.
\item The induced map $\mathcal{B}_n(p)\to B$ is a fiber bundle with fiber $\mathcal{B}_n(F)$ and structure group $K$, provided $B$ is a CW complex and $F$ locally compact.
\end{enumerate}
More specifically, if $\{k_{\alpha\beta}\}$ is a $K$-cocycle for $p$ defined on the trivializing cover $\{U_\alpha\}$, then it is also a $K$-cocycle for each of the resulting fiber bundles.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The first claim is essentially~\cite[Prop. 1]{Sch}, and the second follows from~\cite[Cor. 4.8, Lem. 4.10]{KW1}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem: section space}
For any group $K$ and $K$-space $X$, the homotopy fixed point space $X^{hK}$ is canonically weakly equivalent to the space of sections of the canonical map $EK\times_K X\to BK$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
For the first inequality, Lemmas~\ref{lem: secat homotopy} and~\ref{lem: path space borel} imply that $\operatorname{{\mathsf{dTC}}}_r(G)$ is the distributional sectional category of the projection from $EG^r/G$ to $BG^r$, which, via Lemma~\ref{lem: cosets}, we may identify with the projection from the Borel construction $EG^r\times_{G^r} G^{r-1}$. Appealing to Example~\ref{ex: simplex} and Lemma~\ref{lem: fiber bundles}, we find that $\operatorname{{\mathsf{dTC}}}_r(G)$ is the minimal $n$ for which the bundle $EG^r\times_{G^r} \Delta^{G^{r-1}}_{n}$ over $BG^r$ admits a section---here, we use that $\mathcal{B}_{n+1}(X)\cong \Delta^X_{n}$ for $X$ discrete. By Lemma~\ref{lem: section space}, the existence of such a section is equivalent to non-vacuity of $(\Delta_n^{G^{r-1}})^{hG^r}$, and the claim now follows from Theorem~\ref{thm: classifying model}, since $\Delta^{G^{r-1}}$ maps to its barycentric subdivision in a cellular and equivariant manner.

The proof of the equality $\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_r(G)=\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{\mathcal{D}_r}(G^r)$ follows this argument very closely. The same lemmas permit us to deal with the Borel construction rather than the path space, and, since the base space is a CW complex, hence paracompact, Lemmas~\ref{lem: join secat} and~\ref{lem: fiber bundles} imply that the number in question is the minimal $n$ for which the bundle $EG^r\times_{G^r} (G^{r-1})^{\star (n+1)}$ over $BG^r$ admits a section. By Lemma~\ref{lem: section space} and Theorem~\ref{thm: fglo}, it now suffices to argue that $(G^{r-1})^{\star (n+1)}$ admits a homotopy fixed point if and only if $(G^{r-1})^{\star\infty}_n$ does so. The ``only if'' direction is immediate, since the former space is canonically and equivariantly a subspace of the latter, while the ``if'' direction follows from the equivariant Whitehead theorem as in~\cite[4.11]{FO}

The proof of the second inequality follows in the same manner from~\cite[Prop. 2.1]{KW2} and Proposition~\ref{prop: simplex over G}. Finally, in view of Example~\ref{example: trivial family cd}, the equality $\operatorname{{\mathsf{cat}}}(G)=\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_{\{1\}}(G)$ is equivalent to the Eilenberg--Ganea theorem~\cite{EG}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm: homotopy fixed points} and Corollary~\ref{cor: general subgroup lower bound}, it suffices to show that $K$ contains no elements of the form $(g,g_\sigma)$ with $1\neq \sigma\in \Sigma_T$ for $T\subseteq G^{r-1}$ a finite subset. Supposing otherwise, setting $n=|\sigma|$, and appealing to the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop: subgroup}, we find that $(g,g_\sigma)^n=(g^n, (g^n)_{\textup{id}})$ which lies in a conjugate of the diagonal by Proposition~\ref{prop: diagonal equivalence}. It follows that $(g,g_\sigma)^n$ is trivial by our assumption on $K$, so $g^n=1$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
We say that the group $G$ is $r$-\emph{permutable} for some $r>1$ if there is a finite subset $T\subseteq G^{r-1}$, a nontrivial permutation $\sigma\in \Sigma_T$, and an element $g\in G$ of type $\sigma$. We say that $G$ is \emph{impermutable} if $G$ is not $r$-permutable for some $r>1$.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem: permutability}
The group $G$ is $r$-permutable for some $r>1$ if and only if $r$-permutable for every $r>1$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
It suffices to show, for fixed $r$, that $G$ is $r$-permutable if and only if $2$-permutable. 

Assuming $2$-permutability, and given $g$ of nontrivial type $\sigma\in \Sigma_T$ with $T\subseteq G$, let $\widehat T=\{\widehat x\mid x\in T\}\subseteq G^{r-1}$. Via the diagonal homomorphism, the sets $T$ and $\widehat T$ are canonically in bijection, so $\sigma$ determines a nontrivial permutation $\widehat \sigma$ of $\widehat T$, and an immediate verification shows that $g$ is of type $\widehat \sigma$.

                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
Assume instead that $G$ is $r$-permutable, and choose $g$ of nontrivial type $\sigma\in \Sigma_T$ with $T\subseteq G^{r-1}$. For $x\in T$, let $n(x)$ be the least natural number such that the first coordinates $\sigma^{n(x)}(x)_1$ and $x_1$ coincide. Note that $n(x)$ is bounded above by $|\sigma|$, and, without loss of generality, since $\sigma$ is nontrivial, we have $n(x)>1$ for some $x\in T$. Among all elements of $T$ satisfying this condition, choose $x$ with $n(x)$ minimal. By minimality, the first coordinates $\sigma^{j-1}(x)_1$ are distinct for $1\leq j\leq n(x)$. Writing $S\subseteq G$ for the set of these first coordinates, a direct verification shows that $g$ is of type $\rho$, where $\rho\in \Sigma_S\cong\Sigma_{n(x)}$ is the standard $n(x)$-cycle. Since $n(x)>1$, the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop: impermutable families}
If $G$ is impermutable, then $\mathcal{D}_r={\mathcal P}_r$ for every $r>1$.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The claim is immediate from Proposition~\ref{prop: diagonal equivalence} and Lemma~\ref{lem: permutability}.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor: impermutable consequence}
If $G$ is impermutable, then $\operatorname{{\mathsf{TC}}}_r(G)=\operatorname{{\mathsf{dTC}}}_r(G)$ for every $r>1$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop: impermutable properties}
Let $G$ be a group.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $G$ is impermutable, then $G$ is torsion-free.
\item If $G$ is a subgroup of an impermutable group, then $G$ is impermutable.
\item If $G$ is a finite product of impermutable groups, then $G$ is impermutable.
\item If $G$ is residually impermutable, then $G$ is impermutable.
\item If $G$ is Frobenius injective, then $G$ is impermutable. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
For the first claim, given $g\in G$ with finite order $n$, set $T=\{1, g, \ldots, g^{n-1}\}$. A direct verification shows that $g$ has type $\rho$, where $\rho\in \Sigma_T\cong\Sigma_n$ is the standard $n$ cycle. Since $G$ is impermutable, it follows that $n=1$, which is to say that $g=1$, so $G$ is torsion-free.

The second claim is essentially immediate, and the third may be proved by adapting the argument of Lemma~\ref{lem: permutability}. For the fourth, fix a finite subset $T\subseteq G$ and $g\in G$ of type $\sigma\in \Sigma_T$. For each $x\neq y\in T$, our assumption guarantees a homomorphism $\varphi_{x,y}:G\to K_{x,y}$ such that $K_{x,y}$ is impermutable and $\varphi_{x,y}(xy^{-1})\neq 1$. Writing $K=\prod_{x\neq y\in T} K_{x,y}$, we obtain a homomorphism $\varphi: G\to K$ such that $\varphi|_T$ is injective. Thus, we may view $\sigma$ as a permutation of $\varphi(T)$, and it follows that $\varphi(g)$ has type $\sigma$. Since $K$ is impermutable by (3), it follows that $\sigma$ is trivial.

The fifth claim is essentially due to~\cite{Dr2}, but we give an argument here nevertheless. Fix $T\subseteq G$, a permutation $\sigma\in \Sigma_T$, and an element $g\in G$ of type $\sigma$. Without loss of generality, $\sigma$ is an $n$-cycle, and we write $T=\{x_1,\ldots, x_n\}$ accordingly. By definition, we have $g_\sigma=x_{j+1}^{-1} g x_j$ for any $j$, where the indices are taken modulo $n$. Multiplying these $n$ many distinct but equal expressions in the appropriate order, we conclude that \[(x_{2}^{-1}gx_1)^n=g_\sigma^n=x_1^{-1}g^nx_1=(x_1^{-1}g x_1)^n.\] Invoking Frobenius injectivity and rearranging, we find that $x_1=x_2$, implying that $n=1$ and $\sigma$ is trivial.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor: impermutable list}
The class of impermutable groups contains the classes of torsion-free nilpotent, torsion-free hyperbolic, uniquely divisible, and bi-orderable groups, as well as the class of groups residually in any of these classes.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
As explained in~\cite{Dr2}, the first three types of groups are Frobenius injective, so it remains to show that bi-orderable groups are also Frobenius injective. Given $x,y\in G$ with $G$ bi-orderable, we may assume that $x<y$, and an easy induction shows that $x^n<y^n$ for every $n>0$, so $x^n\neq y^n$ by irreflexivity.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop: klein}
The fundamental group of the Klein bottle is not impermutable.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Recall that the group in question is $K=\langle a,b\mid a^b=a^{-1}\rangle$. Setting $T=\{a,a^{-1}\}$ and writing $\sigma\in\Sigma_T$ for the unique nontrivial permutation, we claim that $b$ is of type $\sigma$. Indeed, we have
\begin{align*}
\sigma(a)\sigma(a^{-1})^{-1}b&=a^{-2}b
=ba^{2}
=ba(a^{-1})^{-1}\\
\sigma(a^{-1})\sigma(a)^{-1}b&=a^{2}b
=ba^{-2}
=ba^{-1}a^{-1},
\end{align*}
as required by the definition.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop: cw failure}
Let $G$ be a group. For any $r>1$, the simplex $\Delta^{G^{r-1}}$ is a $G^r$-complex if and only if $G$ is impermutable.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Suppose there exist a finite subset $T\subseteq G^{r-1}$, a nontrivial permutation $\sigma\in \Sigma_T$, and an element $g\in G$ of type $\sigma$. Then $(\hat g, g_\sigma)$ stabilizes the barycenter of the open simplex spanned by $T$, but it does not fix this simplex pointwise, since it permutes its vertices nontrivially. The conclusion now follows from Proposition~\ref{prop: G-CW criterion}. Conversely, suppose that $G$ is impermutable and that $(g,h)\cdot \mu$ lies in the same open simplex as $\mu$, say the simplex spanned by $T\subseteq G^{r-1}$. Writing $\mu=\sum_{x\in T}t_x x$, we have
\begin{align*}
(g,h)\cdot \mu &= \sum_{x\in T}t_x (\widehat gxh^{-1})
=\sum_{x\in T}s_x x.
\end{align*} Without loss of generality, the barycentric coordinates $t_x$ and $s_x$ are all nonzero, and it follows that the formula $\sigma(x)=\widehat gxh^{-1}$ defines a permutation $\sigma\in \Sigma_T$. A direct verification shows that $g$ has type $\sigma$, whence $\sigma=\textup{id}$ by impermutability; in particular, it follows that $(g,h)$ fixes the vertices of the simplex spanned by $T$, hence the entire simplex. The conclusion now follows from Proposition~\ref{prop: G-CW criterion}.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
We do not know whether the converses to Proposition~\ref{prop: impermutable families}, Corollary~\ref{cor: impermutable consequence}, or Proposition~\ref{prop: impermutable properties}(5) hold.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
